steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our visualization paper presenting NOVA, an interactive interface that helps members of the public assess their own beliefs about bias in news media coverage. Motivate the problem of media bias, explain why automated bias detection falls short, describe our guided, belief-centered approach, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- News media today and how bias gets in
- Perceived bias, "fake news" and echo chambers
- Computational bias detection and its limits
- Our approach: belief externalization with guided exploration
- NOVA: goal and system
- Audience, workflow, user study, contributions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Today, written news media is a mix of content that is automatically generated by news algorithms and long thematic pieces that journalists curate to give deeper analysis and thorough explanations to the public. At the same time, many methods and different stages of the journalistic process put biases into a news article. How an article is written and framed can have a strong impact on people's opinions and perspectives on issues. Media bias and its effects are widely documented and the general public knows about them.

People often dismiss articles from outlets they see as “biased” as “fake news”. If people keep dismissing other perspectives, this can slowly form an echo chamber, as people insulate themselves inside their personal beliefs without meaning to.

Recent developments in Natural Language Processing have led to more effort to rethink how we analyze media bias. Researchers in social science and psychology have been calling for an interdisciplinary approach with computer science to assess news media content. Previous works have applied machine learning models on annotated datasets to identify some types of media bias, but these have performance issues. One key reason is that it is difficult to build a high-quality bias dataset. Readers cannot agree on what is biased because of factors like background knowledge, political ideology, or even the Hostile Media Effect in psychology. Even with the recent advances in Large Language Models, resolving this issue among readers is still hard.

  - environment where people externalize beliefs, find evidence for/against -> avoids belief conflicts
  - interactive presentation narrative structure: three stages, each with task and instructions

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Today, written news media is a mix of content that is automatically generated by news algorithms and long thematic pieces that journalists curate to give deeper analysis and thorough explanations to the public. At the same time, many methods and different stages of the journalistic process put biases into a news article. How an article is written and framed can have a strong impact on people's opinions and perspectives on issues. Media bias and its effects are widely documented and the general public knows about them.

People often dismiss articles from outlets they see as “biased” as “fake news”. If people keep dismissing other perspectives, this can slowly form an echo chamber, as people insulate themselves inside their personal beliefs without meaning to.

Recent developments in Natural Language Processing have led to more effort to rethink how we analyze media bias. Researchers in social science and psychology have been calling for an interdisciplinary approach with computer science to assess news media content. Previous works have applied machine learning models on annotated datasets to identify some types of media bias, but these have performance issues. One key reason is that it is difficult to build a high-quality bias dataset. Readers cannot agree on what is biased because of factors like background knowledge, political ideology, or even the Hostile Media Effect in psychology. Even with the recent advances in Large Language Models, resolving this issue among readers is still hard.

To address these issues we propose to create an environment where people externalize their beliefs about media biases and find evidence that supports or disproves them. This way belief conflicts among people are avoided. To guide user exploration in this environment, we use the interactive presentation narrative structure and divide the environment into three stages, each one with a clear task and set of instructions. Previous works have reported that “the interpretations of the text can be multiple and they depend on the personal background knowledge, culture, social class, religion, etc. as far as what is normal (expected) and what is not are concerned”. Because beliefs are complex, we guide user exploration with less contentious “signals”, namely sentiment and named entities, building on prior works that showed that combining them can identify framing characteristics. In our work the entities and sentiments point users to potential media biases, but the users have full control over which direction to go and whether an actual bias is found.

We want to explore the relationship between a person's beliefs about news media outlets and how those outlets behave. We take into account the key findings in other fields and introduce an alternative approach to explore and assess whether a person's perception of a media outlet matches how that outlet reported on a topic. To do this we introduce a system for News Outlet Visual Assessment (NOVA). NOVA is a visual interface designed to help with self-assessment of personal beliefs about news media coverage biases.

Our target audience is a subset of the general public. We are aiming at people who either encounter or actively look for news media articles and content (e.g., NYT, CNN, etc) fairly regularly (i.e., at least monthly). We go through an example workflow to show how NOVA can help assess media outlet coverage in relation to a person's beliefs. We also present a user study with a qualitative analysis of how users explore and what challenges they have in assessing personal beliefs. Our contributions are:

- • We introduce NOVA, a multi-stage system that combines presentation narrative structure and belief elicitation so the general public can self-assess their personal belief on news media coverage.

- • We identify lessons learned from designing and evaluating an interactive visualization system for belief elicitation and assessment, and prospective research directions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In the current age, written news media is a combination of content that is either automatically generated by news algorithms [1] or long thematic pieces curated by journalists to provide deeper analysis and thorough explanations to the public. At the same time, many methods and different stages of the journalistic process inject biases into a news article. How an article is written and framed [2] can strongly impact one’s opinions and perspectives on issues. Media bias and its effects are widely documented [3,4,5,6] and known to the general public.

Articles published by outlets people perceive as “biased” are often dismissed as “fake news”. The continued dismissal of other perspectives can gradually form an echo chamber as people unintentionally insulate themselves within their personal beliefs [7].

Recent developments in Natural Language Processing have sparked an increased effort to rethink how we analyze media bias. Social science and psychology researchers have been calling for an interdisciplinary approach with computer science to assess news media content [2]. Previous works have applied machine learning models on annotated datasets to identify certain types of media bias [8,9,10,5], but they are susceptible to performance issues [11,12]. A key reason is the difficulty of building a high-quality bias dataset. Readers are unable to agree on what is biased due to factors like background knowledge, political ideology, or even the Hostile Media Effect in psychology [6]. Even with recent advances in Large Language Models, it remains challenging to resolve this issue among readers.

To address these issues, we propose to create an environment where people externalize their beliefs on media biases and find evidence to support or disprove them. In this way, belief conflicts among people are effectively avoided. To guide user exploration within such an environment, we incorporate the interactive presentation narrative structure [13] by dividing the environment into three stages, each with a clear task and set of instructions. Previous works have reported that “the interpretations of the text can be multiple and they depend on the personal background knowledge, culture, social class, religion, etc. as far as what is normal (expected) and what is not are concerned” [14]. Recognizing the complexity of beliefs, we choose to guide user exploration with less contentious “signals”, i.e., sentiment and named entities, building upon prior works that have shown the viability of combining them to identify framing characteristics [14,15,16,17]. Note that in our work, the entities and sentiments direct users to potential media biases, while the users have full control over which direction to go and whether an actual bias is found.

We are interested in exploring the relationship between one’s personal beliefs about news media outlets and how those outlets behave. Taking into account key findings in other fields, we introduce an alternative approach to explore and assess whether one’s perception of a media outlet aligns with how that outlet reported on a topic. To achieve this, we introduce a system for News Outlet Visual Assessment (NOVA), a visual interface designed to facilitate the self-assessment of personal beliefs on news media coverage biases.

Our target audience is a subset of the general public: individuals who either encounter or actively seek out news media articles and content (e.g., NYT, CNN, etc) fairly regularly (i.e., at least monthly). We walk through an example workflow to demonstrate how NOVA can facilitate assessing media outlet coverage as it relates to one’s personal beliefs. Additionally, we present a user study with a qualitative analysis of user exploration strategies and challenges for personal belief assessment. Our contributions are as follows:

- • We introduce NOVA, a multi-stage system that combines presentation narrative structure and belief elicitation for the general public to self-assess their personal belief on news media coverage.

- • We identify lessons learned from designing and evaluating an interactive visualization system for belief elicitation and assessment, as well as prospective research directions.
